title: MindVLM: Neural-Grounded Visual Captioning via Subject-Aware Semantic Evidence Selection
claim: Supervision text describes content that the input never contained, so the model faces a mismatch between its evidence and the labels.
layout: 2 side-by-side panels, each image above its caption, confused-person icon at bottom center
description: Two tilted, rounded photo cards sit side by side with soft orange glow borders. The left card shows a kite-boarder jumping over rough sea. The right card shows a yellow and blue train with a man standing beside the track. Hatched, dimmed bands at the left and right edges of each photo mark regions cropped out during the experiment. Red dashed boxes sit in the dimmed areas, one around a kite on the left and one around a man holding a flag on the right. Under each photo is an MS-COCO caption with the absent objects in bold red, such as 'kite' and 'holding a flag'. Orange beams run from the captions to a cartoon person at bottom center who shrugs under question marks. The eye goes first to the photos, then to the red boxes and red words.
caption: Examples illustrating semantic mismatches between cropped NSD images and their corresponding MS-COCO captions (see Figure [ref]). Dimmed regions indicate portions of the original image removed during the NSD [ref] neural recording experiment. The \fcolorbox{red}{white}{red dashed boxes} mark objects that are physically absent from the cropped image but still explicitly referenced in the ground-truth captions, resulting in semantic loss, where fMRI signals can only partially capture the full scene semantics. Dataset-level statistics are in Figure [ref].
abstract: Translating visual brain activity into natural language offers a powerful window into human cognition and neural semantic representation. Most prior brain-captioning approaches project fMRI signals into language space using paired supervision. However, the widely used Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) was built based only on image-fMRI pairs, while existing methods rely on MS-COCO captions as indirect textual supervision. Critically, during fMRI acquisition, participants observe only cropped image regions, whereas the associated MS-COCO captions describe full scenes. This mismatch creates a fundamental gap between neural representations and textual supervision, introducing an inherent semantic loss in NSD-based brain captioning. To mitigate this limitation, we reformulate brain captioning as Neural-Grounded Visual Captioning, where language is generated directly from visually grounded neural evidence rather than text supervision. We propose MindVLM, a framework that maps fMRI signals into subject-aware visual tokens and leverages a frozen vision-language model (VLM) to produce interpretable and personalized descriptions. Instead of point-wise regression, MindVLM focuses on extracting semantically relevant visual cues from neural activity, naturally accommodating partial observability and inter-subject variability. Extensive experiments on NSD show that MindVLM maintains, and often improves, caption quality across multiple VLM backbones, including LLaVA-v1.5, Qwen2.5-VL, and Gemma3, beyond intrinsic model priors. Despite requiring neither text supervision nor an LLM during training and operating under an image-grounded inference paradigm distinct from conventional captioning methods, MindVLM remains competitive with supervised approaches, suggesting that subject-specific neural grounding provides an efficient, scalable, and interpretable path toward faithful brain-to-language generation.
